newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's Aznar again rules out talks with ETA.
newsitem.headline: Spain's Aznar again rules out talks with ETA.

text.p: Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar on Monday ruled out peace talks with ETA Basque separatists one day after the guerrilla group's political wing renewed calls for negotiations.

"There is very little to negotiate politically or socially with those who are dedicated to violence or those who defend violence," Aznar told a meeting of his Popular Party's (PP) executive committee in the northern Basque city of Bilbao.

Responding to nationwide outrage at the rebels' killing of a young PP politician earlier this month, ETA's political arm Herri Batasuna held a demonstration in San Sebastian on Sunday where it reiterated support for negotiations.
Herri Batasuna's chief spokesman Floren Aoiz, addressing more than 20,000 supporters, said his party "is holding out its hand in the search for peace".

The separatist guerrillas incensed Spaniards with the abduction and killing of 29-year-old Basque town councillor Miguel Angel Blanco. An estimated six million people took to the streets in protest against ETA in the days following the attack.

Herri Batasuna has long called for peace talks between the central government and the guerrilla group, which has killed some 800 people in nearly three decades of fighting for Basque independence. But Aznar has ruled out negotiations until ETA lays down its arms.
At the demonstration, the group's sympathisers marched peacefully through the scenic Basque coastal town of San Sebastian chanting "Long live the ETA military!" and "Independence".

But hours after the march ended, three people were injured in clashes between youthful supporters of ETA and police. The youths, their faces masked, hurled dozens of petrol bombs at police who responded by firing rubber bullets into the air.
Aznar summoned the conservative party's leadership to a meeting in the Basque region for the first time on Monday.
He has been trying to capitalise on strong anti-ETA sentiment in the region over Blanco's killing in hopes of bringing more pressure on the group.

Blanco, who held an unpaid post in the Popular Party, was killed after the government refused demands to immediately move some 500 ETA prisoners serving sentences around Spain to jails in the Basque country.
The killing and the massive outcry it triggered were a turning point which saw Basques, once intimidated by the radicals, condemning them openly.
Aznar and political leaders in the Basque country branded Herri Batasuna an "accomplice" to Blanco's killing.
The premier reiterated on Monday a pledge to isolate Herri Batasuna, a political party which got about 15 percent of the vote in the most recent Basque regional elections.
"Those who pull the trigger and those who help them must see what political rejection means every day," Aznar said.
He added that legal reforms promised as part of a crackdown on ETA and its supporters could be ready by mid-August.
The reforms would outlaw some types of demonstrations by the radicals and would criminalise anything construed as defence of terrorism.
